# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Vaikiv Therapeutics, Inc. / Taigon Pharma Holdings, LLC: Oravexin APA document set, buyer-side issues for markup
**Date:** November 10, 2026

---

## Executive Summary

Vaikiv is buying the Oravexin 40 mg extended-release tablet franchise (NDA 214-883) for a **Purchase Price of $186,000,000** (APA §2.6). The deal includes an **$18,600,000** indemnity escrow (Escrow Agreement §2.1), a cap of 10% of the Purchase Price ($18.6 million) and a $1,395,000 Deductible (APA §9.5(a)).

Each document reads acceptably on its own. Read together, three provisions take away protection Vaikiv appears to have:

1. **Survival of the regulatory and product-quality reps is about 90 days.** APA §9.1 ties survival to the escrow "Release Date," and Escrow Agreement §4.1 sets that date at 90 days after Closing.
2. **The TSA moves APA disputes to New York.** TSA §9.3 applies New York law and New York courts to disputes "relating to … the Purchase Agreement." The APA's own precedence clause (§11.4) does not cure this, because it lets each Ancillary Agreement control matters arising under it.
3. **The known 2025 recall is back under the cap and deductible.** Schedule 2.4(c) uses the express hook in APA §2.4(c) to override the uncapped Excluded Liability carve-out in §9.5(b) for the 2025 Oravexin recall.

Issues 1 and 3 together are the most serious. They leave Vaikiv with a short window for unknown quality problems and a capped, shared recovery for the one quality problem everyone already knows about.

Secondary points and items needing client or business input follow the main issues.

---

## Issue 1: Seller's regulatory and product-quality reps survive only about 90 days

**Where:**
- APA §9.1 (Survival), read with APA §1.1 ("Release Date" has the meaning given in the Escrow Agreement).
- Escrow Agreement §4.1 (Release Date).

**What the documents do:**
- APA §9.1 provides that Seller's non-fundamental reps, "including the representations and warranties in Sections 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7," survive "**until the Release Date (as defined in the Escrow Agreement)**." Those sections cover regulatory and FDCA/cGMP compliance, product quality and stability, and recalls.
- §9.1 also bars any §9.2(a) claim not noticed before the survival period expires.
- Escrow Agreement §4.1 defines the Release Date as "**ninety (90) days after the Closing Date**," rolled to the next Business Day.
- On the draft's March 2, 2026 Closing Date, 90 days falls on Sunday, May 31, 2026. The Release Date would therefore be Monday, June 1, 2026.
- §9.1 states that the parties intend the survival periods to shorten the statute of limitations under **10 Del. C. § 8106(c)**. Delaware courts enforce that kind of contractual shortening.

**Why it matters to Vaikiv:**
- **The window is too short.** The risks this asset actually carries are latent. They include:
  - stability failures that appear at the 12-, 18- or 24-month time points;
  - cGMP problems that surface at the next FDA inspection of Brennholt's Raleigh facility;
  - inaccurate past FDA submissions;
  - adverse event trends.
- **The product's history shows the risk is real.** The 2025 Recall was triggered by an out-of-specification result at the **12-month** stability point (Schedule 2.4(c)). A 90-day survival period would not have captured an equivalent problem.
- **The reps become largely illusory.** Rep-breach claims under §9.2(a) on §§4.5–4.7 would expire before these problems normally emerge. §9.7 (exclusive remedy) blocks any fallback claim outside Article IX, other than Fraud.
- **The cash leaves at the same time.** The escrow pays out to Seller on the same 90-day timetable. Taigon is an LLC holding company, so collection risk rises sharply after release.
- **The cross-reference is easy to miss.** Neither document shows the problem on its face. The 90-day number appears only in the Escrow Agreement, which the escrow agent will treat as administrative.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Give the APA its own survival periods.** Do not key survival to any escrow date. Market for a pharma asset deal is 18–24 months for general reps, with longer periods for regulatory and product-quality reps.
- **Key the escrow release to the APA survival period**, not the other way around. Consider a staged release, for example 50% at 12 months and the balance at the general survival expiry, less pending claims.
- **Proposed APA §9.1 language:**

  > "The representations and warranties of Seller in Article IV, other than the Fundamental Representations and the Regulatory Representations, shall survive the Closing until the date that is twenty-four (24) months after the Closing Date. The representations and warranties in Sections 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 (the "**Regulatory Representations**") shall survive the Closing until the date that is thirty-six (36) months after the Closing Date. The survival periods in this Section 9.1 shall not be determined by reference to, or be affected by, the Release Date or any other provision of the Escrow Agreement."

- **Conforming Escrow Agreement §4.1:**

  > "The "**Release Date**" means the date on which the survival period applicable to the representations and warranties of Seller (other than the Fundamental Representations and the Regulatory Representations) under Section 9.1 of the Purchase Agreement expires …"

- **Housekeeping:** delete the APA §1.1 definition that imports "Release Date" from the Escrow Agreement, or reverse it so the escrow imports the definition from the APA.

---

## Issue 2: TSA §9.3 moves APA-related disputes to New York law and New York courts

**Where:**
- TSA §9.3 (Governing Law; Jurisdiction).
- APA §§11.8 and 11.9 (Delaware law; exclusive Court of Chancery forum).
- APA §11.4 (precedence).

**What the documents do:**
- **The APA picks Delaware.** APA §11.8 applies Delaware law to all claims "arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the transactions contemplated by it." APA §11.9 gives the **Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware** exclusive jurisdiction. The Escrow Agreement (§§10.1–10.2) matches.
- **The TSA picks New York, for the APA too.** TSA §9.3 applies "**the laws of the State of New York**" to any dispute "arising out of or relating to this Agreement **or the Purchase Agreement**." It gives exclusive jurisdiction to the state and federal courts in New York County, again "for any action arising out of or relating to this Agreement **or the Purchase Agreement**," and includes a covenant not to sue elsewhere.
- **The precedence clause does not resolve the conflict.** APA §11.4 says the APA prevails over Ancillary Agreements, **"except that each Ancillary Agreement shall control with respect to matters arising under such Ancillary Agreement."** The TSA is an Ancillary Agreement. Any dispute that arises under the TSA is therefore governed by TSA §9.3, which by its terms reaches APA claims as well.

**Why it matters to Vaikiv:**
- **Most early disputes will straddle both agreements.** The transition period is when the most likely disputes arise. Examples:
  - **Batch release:** a batch released by Seller's quality unit under TSA §5.3 that later fails. This is a TSA claim and also an APA §4.6 or §4.11 claim.
  - **Regulatory reporting:** Seller's handling of the open 2025 Recall, the Form 483 follow-up or field alert reports while it still holds the NDA (TSA §5.1, Schedule A-1). This is a TSA claim and also an APA §4.5 or §6.3 claim.
  - **Recall costs:** TSA §5.4 expressly sends recall costs back to APA §6.4.
  - **Inventory quality** at transfer (Schedule A-4 and APA §4.11).
- **Seller can split or move the dispute.** In each of these cases, Seller can argue the matter "arises under" the TSA, so New York law and forum control the whole dispute, including the APA claim. That exposes Vaikiv to:
  - **parallel proceedings** in Delaware Chancery and New York County on one economic dispute;
  - **forum-selection motion practice** before reaching the merits;
  - **inconsistent law**, for example on enforcement of the §8106(c) survival shortening, sandbagging and implied covenant arguments;
  - a jury-waiver gap, because TSA §9.4 covers only the TSA.
- **The TSA liability cap could leak into APA claims.** TSA §8.3 caps liability at total Service Fees. Seller could argue that cap applies to any loss framed as a TSA performance failure. Moving the APA claim into a TSA forum makes that argument easier.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Preferred: conform the TSA to Delaware.** Replace TSA §9.3 with a clause mirroring APA §§11.8–11.9:

  > "**9.3 Governing Law; Jurisdiction.** This Agreement, and all claims or causes of action arising out of or relating to this Agreement, shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the internal laws of the State of Delaware, without giving effect to any choice or conflict of law provision or rule that would cause the application of the laws of any other jurisdiction. Section 11.9 (Exclusive Forum) and Section 11.10 (Waiver of Jury Trial) of the Purchase Agreement shall apply to this Agreement, *mutatis mutandis*."

- **Fallback, if Taigon insists on New York for pure TSA service disputes:**
  - delete "or the Purchase Agreement" in both places in TSA §9.3; and
  - add: "Notwithstanding the foregoing, any claim, controversy or dispute that arises out of or relates to the Purchase Agreement, including any claim that also arises under this Agreement, shall be governed exclusively by Sections 11.8 and 11.9 of the Purchase Agreement."
- **Amend APA §11.4** so the exception cannot be used against the APA's dispute provisions:

  > "… except that each Ancillary Agreement shall control with respect to matters arising solely under such Ancillary Agreement; *provided* that Sections 9.1, 9.5, 11.8, 11.9 and 11.10 of this Agreement shall prevail over any provision of any Ancillary Agreement."

- **Clarify TSA §8.3** so the TSA cap does not limit any claim under the Purchase Agreement.

---

## Issue 3: Schedule 2.4(c) puts Seller's liability for the known 2025 recall back under the cap and deductible

**Where:**
- Seller Disclosure Schedule, **Schedule 2.4(c)**, ¶3 ("Treatment").
- APA §2.4(c), §9.5(a)–(b), §11.4 and §11.12.

**What the documents do:**
- **The APA makes recall liabilities uncapped.**
  - APA §2.4(c) makes pre-Closing product liability and recall Liabilities Excluded Liabilities, "**except to the extent provided in Schedule 2.4(c)**."
  - APA §9.5(b) removes Excluded Liabilities (§9.2(c)) from the Cap and the Deductible.
- **The Schedule takes that protection back for the 2025 Recall.** Schedule 2.4(c) describes the 2025 voluntary Class II recall of Lots OX-2511 through OX-2519 (Recall Event No. 94417). It confirms the related Liabilities are Excluded Liabilities, but then provides that Seller's §9.2(c) indemnity for them "shall be **subject to the Cap and the Deductible under Section 9.5 notwithstanding Section 9.5(b)**."
- **The APA's own terms support the Schedule.**
  - §2.4(c) expressly delegates to the Schedule.
  - §11.12 incorporates the Disclosure Schedule into the APA.
  - The Schedule therefore operates as a negotiated APA term, not a conflicting document, and the "APA prevails" language in §11.4 does not override it.
  - Seller will argue the specific Schedule language controls the general carve-out in §9.5(b).

**Why it matters to Vaikiv:**
- **A known Seller liability becomes a capped, shared one.** The 2025 Recall is a known, pre-Closing liability that should sit entirely with Seller. Under the current drafting:
  - Vaikiv absorbs the first **$1,395,000** of recall Losses, because the Deductible is aggregated with all other §9.2(a)-type claims;
  - recovery is limited to the **$18.6 million** Cap;
  - that same $18.6 million must cover **every other capped claim**, including any rep breaches.
- **The recall is not closed.** Per the Schedule:
  - Seller has received returns for only about 81% of distributed units;
  - FDA has not terminated the recall;
  - the CAPA plan is still before FDA.
  
  Open exposure includes retrieval, credits, regulatory response costs and product liability claims on the roughly 19% of units still in the market.
- **The cap may effectively shrink further.** If Issue 1 is not fixed, the escrow releases around June 1, 2026. Vaikiv would then pursue capped recall claims directly against Taigon.
- **There is no fallback route.** Schedule 4.7 discloses the 2025 Recall against the §4.7 recall rep, so Vaikiv has no rep-breach claim for it. The Excluded Liability indemnity is the **only** protection.
- **Seller also keeps the insurance money.** Schedule 2.2, item 4, makes Seller's insurance proceeds for the 2025 Recall an Excluded Asset. Seller keeps the insurance recovery while capping its indemnity to Vaikiv.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Delete the second sentence of Schedule 2.4(c) ¶3** in full, so 2025 Recall Liabilities remain **uncapped Excluded Liabilities** under §9.5(b).
- **Close the delegation in APA §2.4(c)** so future schedule drafting cannot repeat this:

  > "(c) all Liabilities arising out of or relating to product liability claims, recalls, market withdrawals, field corrections or similar actions with respect to units of the Product manufactured, distributed or sold before the Closing (including the 2025 Recall described in Schedule 2.4(c)). Nothing in the Disclosure Schedule shall limit, qualify or modify the scope of any Excluded Liability or the application of Section 9.5(b)."

- **Add to APA §9.5(b):**

  > "This Section 9.5(b) shall apply notwithstanding any contrary provision of the Disclosure Schedule or any Ancillary Agreement."

- **Supporting asks:**
  - a specific line-item indemnity for the 2025 Recall, sitting outside the escrow waterfall in §9.6 so recall claims do not drain the escrow;
  - Seller's undertaking to pursue its insurance for recall Losses; or
  - deletion of item 4 of Schedule 2.2 so Vaikiv shares in those proceeds.

---

## Secondary Points for the Markup

**A. Escrow sizing and waterfall (APA §§2.7, 9.6; Escrow Agreement §4).**
- The escrow equals the Cap, and §9.6 sends all §9.2 claims to the escrow first, including uncapped Excluded Liability claims.
- Uncapped claims can therefore consume escrow intended for rep claims.
- **Ask:** uncapped claims (Excluded Liabilities, Fraud) may be recovered directly from Seller at Buyer's election. Also link the release mechanics to the corrected survival periods (see Issue 1).

**B. TSA liability cap and indemnity standard (TSA §§8.1, 8.3).**
- Seller indemnifies TSA performance only for gross negligence, willful misconduct or fraud, breach of §5 or §6, or legal violation.
- Aggregate liability is capped at Service Fees, roughly $1.9 million over nine months excluding A-6.
- Batch release (TSA §5.3) is a high-consequence service.
- **Ask:** carve batch-release and pharmacovigilance failures out of the TSA cap, or set a higher dedicated cap. Confirm the TSA cap does not limit APA claims.

**C. Recall-related regulatory obligations during the TSA period.**
- Seller remains NDA holder until FDA acknowledges the transfer, and the 2025 Recall and Form 483 follow-up are still open (Schedule 4.5).
- **Ask:** an express covenant that Seller will drive the 2025 Recall to FDA termination at its own cost. Recall support under Schedule A-6 is currently billed to Vaikiv at $225/hour; recall-support time for the 2025 Recall should be at Seller's cost.

**D. Closing press release (D5).**
- No legal issue identified.
- The release is consistent with the APA on price, assets, NDA number and TSA term.
- Confirm that business is comfortable with the "durable patent position" statement. The pending application and two Orange Book patents are listed, but the release should not get ahead of any patent diligence conclusions.
- The release is a joint release under APA §6.7, so it needs Taigon sign-off.

---

## Items Requiring Client or Business Team Input

1. **Target survival periods.**
   - Confirm Vaikiv's position on survival: our proposal is 24 months general and 36 months for §§4.5–4.7.
   - Confirm whether the business wants a staged escrow release.
   - This depends on Vaikiv's own quality and CMC diligence on Brennholt and on how much leverage the team wants to spend.
2. **Recall exposure estimate.**
   - We need regulatory and quality to estimate remaining 2025 Recall costs, covering the roughly 19% of units not yet returned, FDA close-out and any product liability tail.
   - This tells us whether to hold firm on fully uncapped treatment or accept a separate, higher recall-specific cap as a fallback.
   - Our recommendation is uncapped.
3. **Seller credit support.**
   - Taigon is an LLC holding company. Ask whether the business team knows its balance sheet after the sale and whether a parent guaranty or a larger escrow is realistic.
   - This matters most for uncapped Excluded Liability claims that fall outside the escrow.
4. **New York forum for pure TSA disputes.**
   - Is there any business reason, such as Taigon's operations or counsel being in New York, to accept the fallback (New York for service-level disputes only)?
   - The alternative is to insist on full Delaware conformity.
5. **TSA risk tolerance.**
   - Confirm acceptable liability levels for batch release and pharmacovigilance services, and the timing for Vaikiv's quality unit to take over release. Schedule A-3 ends at six months.
6. **Timeline and dates.**
   - The drafts assume a February 9, 2026 signing, a March 2, 2026 Closing and an April 30, 2026 outside date (APA §8.1(b)).
   - Confirm the current timetable so we can roll all dates forward consistently across the APA, Escrow Agreement, TSA and press release in the markup.
7. **Insurance.**
   - Does Vaikiv want to pursue sharing of Seller's 2025 Recall insurance proceeds (Schedule 2.2, item 4)?
   - Or would the business prefer to trade that point for full uncapped indemnity?

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Vaikiv Therapeutics, Inc. / Taigon Pharma Holdings, LLC: Oravexin APA document review, buyer-side issues
**Documents reviewed:** Asset Purchase Agreement (APA); Indemnity Escrow Agreement (Escrow); Seller Disclosure Schedule (DS); Transition Services Agreement (TSA); Joint Closing Press Release

---

## Executive Summary

Vaikiv is buying the Oravexin 40 mg extended-release tablet franchise (NDA 214-883) for **$186,000,000**. The APA was signed February 9, 2026 and closing is scheduled for March 2, 2026. The headline economics are conventional:

- an $18.6 million escrow;
- a 10% cap on general rep claims, with a $1,395,000 deductible;
- Delaware law and Delaware Chancery as the forum.

Two of the most significant problems only show up when the documents are read against each other:

1. **Survival is effectively 90 days.** The APA does not set its own survival period for Seller's general representations. It borrows the Escrow "Release Date," and the Escrow sets that date at 90 days after Closing. This covers the regulatory, cGMP, product-quality and recall representations. Rep-breach claims for latent manufacturing or FDA issues would expire around June 1, 2026.
2. **The TSA overrides the APA's Delaware law and forum.** The TSA pulls disputes "relating to" the APA into New York law and New York courts. The APA's own conflicts clause does not cure this.

I also note several secondary points for the markup. They are below in order of significance.

---

## Issue 1: Survival of Seller's representations ends 90 days after Closing

**Where:**
- APA § 9.1 (Survival), read with the APA § 1.1 definition of "Release Date."
- Escrow § 4.1 (Release Date).

**What the documents say:**
- **APA § 9.1.** Seller's non-fundamental representations "including the representations and warranties in Sections 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7" survive "until the Release Date (as defined in the Escrow Agreement)." No claim under § 9.2(a) may be brought unless noticed before that date.
- **Escrow § 4.1.** The Release Date is "the date that is ninety (90) days after the Closing Date," rolled to the next Business Day.
- **The resulting date.** On a March 2, 2026 Closing, day 90 is Sunday, May 31, 2026. The Release Date is therefore **Monday, June 1, 2026**.
- **Express intent to shorten.** § 9.1 states that the parties intend the survival periods to shorten the statute of limitations under 10 Del. C. § 8106(c). A Delaware court will enforce that.

**Why it matters to Vaikiv:**
- **The affected representations are the core diligence protections for a pharma asset.** They are:
  - § 4.5: NDA status, FDA submissions, cGMP compliance, and the absence of 483s and warning letters;
  - § 4.6: product quality, adulteration and misbranding, stability data, and uninvestigated OOS/OOT results;
  - § 4.7: no other recalls, and no facts reasonably expected to lead to one.
- **The problems these reps cover surface slowly.** Latent manufacturing and stability defects typically appear on a 12–24 month horizon, through:
  - stability time points (the 2025 OOS result appeared at the 12-month point);
  - FDA re-inspection of the CMO;
  - adverse event trends;
  - annual report review.
- **The known history makes the window more dangerous, not less.** The CMO received a June 2025 Form 483 that included an in-process moisture observation (DS Sched. 4.5), and Inventory will be drawn from CMO production. A 90-day window gives Vaikiv essentially no protection on the reps it most needs.
- **The claim bar, not just escrow access, is the problem.** Once the Release Date passes, the escrow is released to Seller and any unnoticed rep claim is extinguished outright, not merely left without escrow security.
- **The escrow mechanics compound it.** Escrow § 4.2(a) only permits Claim Notices before the Release Date, so escrow access closes at the same time.

**Recommended fix:**
- Give the APA its own survival periods and stop relying on the Escrow definition.
- Re-tie the escrow release to the APA general survival period, with a possible partial step-down.

Proposed APA § 9.1 language:

> "The representations and warranties of Seller in Article IV, other than the Fundamental Representations and the Regulatory Representations, shall survive the Closing until the date that is twenty-four (24) months after the Closing Date. The representations and warranties in Sections 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 (the "**Regulatory Representations**") shall survive the Closing until the date that is thirty-six (36) months after the Closing Date. [Fundamental Representations: unchanged.]"

Conforming changes:
- Delete the APA § 1.1 definition of "Release Date" as a cross-reference. Alternatively, keep it only for escrow mechanics and make clear it has no bearing on survival.
- Amend Escrow § 4.1 so that the Release Date is the date on which the general survival period under APA § 9.1 expires (e.g., "the date that is [eighteen (18) / twenty-four (24)] months after the Closing Date"). Consider a 50% release at 12 months, net of Pending Claim Amounts.
- Market fallback: 18 months for general reps and 24–36 months for the Regulatory Representations. Do not accept anything shorter than 12 months for §§ 4.5–4.7.

---

## Issue 2: The TSA imposes New York law and New York courts on disputes "relating to" the APA

**Where:** TSA § 9.3 (Governing Law; Jurisdiction), set against APA § 11.8 (Delaware law), APA § 11.9 (exclusive Delaware Court of Chancery forum) and APA § 11.4 (Conflicts with Ancillary Agreements).

**What the documents say:**
- **APA §§ 11.8 and 11.9.** All claims arising out of or relating to the APA or the transactions are governed by Delaware law and go exclusively to the Court of Chancery.
- **Escrow §§ 10.1 and 10.2.** These are consistent with the APA.
- **TSA § 9.3.** It covers any dispute "arising out of or relating to this Agreement *or the Purchase Agreement*." It selects:
  - New York law; and
  - the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County.

  Each party agrees not to sue elsewhere.
- **APA § 11.4.** The APA prevails over Ancillary Agreements, "except that each Ancillary Agreement shall control with respect to matters arising under such Ancillary Agreement." The TSA is an Ancillary Agreement (APA § 1.1).

**Why it matters to Vaikiv:**
- **The precedence clause does not resolve the conflict.** The § 11.4 exception means the TSA controls TSA matters, so TSA § 9.3 governs at least every TSA dispute in New York.
- **Seller has a plausible argument that the TSA clause reaches APA claims too.** TSA § 9.3 expressly purports to cover APA disputes. Seller can argue that any APA claim connected to transition services is a "matter arising under" the TSA. Examples:
  - a defective batch released by Seller's quality unit under TSA § 5.3;
  - a late field alert report or adverse event report under TSA § 5.2;
  - Inventory quality;
  - recall support under TSA § 5.4 and Sched. A-6.
- **The overlap is unusually large in this deal.** For the first six to nine months, Seller runs batch release, pharmacovigilance and regulatory submissions. Most operational problems in that period will have both an APA rep or indemnity angle and a TSA performance angle.
- **The practical result is split proceedings.** We could see:
  - parallel actions in Chancery and New York County;
  - a threshold forum fight Seller can use to delay;
  - inconsistent law on one economic dispute (for example, New York and Delaware differ on sandbagging, implied covenant scope and limitations treatment);
  - a risk that the § 8106(c) analysis and the APA's limitations provisions are argued under New York law.
- **The TSA terms are worse for Vaikiv.** TSA § 8.3 caps liability at Service Fees, roughly $220,000 per month in fixed fees. TSA § 8.1 indemnity is limited to gross negligence or wilful misconduct, breach of § 5 or § 6, and violation of law. Seller would prefer to have Vaikiv's claims characterized as TSA claims for these reasons too.

**Recommended fix:** The preferred approach is to conform the TSA to the APA.

> "**9.3 Governing Law; Jurisdiction.** This Agreement shall be governed by, and disputes arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall be resolved in accordance with, Sections 11.8 (Governing Law), 11.9 (Exclusive Forum) and 11.10 (Waiver of Jury Trial) of the Purchase Agreement, which are incorporated herein *mutatis mutandis*."

If Seller insists on New York for pure TSA service disputes, accept that only on the following terms:
- Delete "or the Purchase Agreement" in both sentences of TSA § 9.3.
- Add to TSA § 9.3:

  > "Notwithstanding the foregoing, any claim, controversy or dispute arising out of or relating to the Purchase Agreement (including any claim for indemnification under Article IX thereof, whether or not related to the Services) shall be governed exclusively by Sections 11.8 and 11.9 of the Purchase Agreement."
- Amend APA § 11.4 to add:

  > "provided, however, that Sections 9.1, 11.8 and 11.9 of this Agreement shall prevail over any provision of any Ancillary Agreement."

---

## Issue 3: TSA liability cap and indemnity scope are thin for regulatory-critical services

**Where:** TSA §§ 8.1, 8.3; Schedule A (A-1 to A-7).

**Why it matters to Vaikiv:**
- **The cap is small relative to the exposure.** Aggregate liability is capped at "total Service Fees paid and payable." Over a nine-month term that is roughly $2.0 million of fixed fees. Seller performs batch release (TSA § 5.3) and pharmacovigilance reporting (TSA § 5.2), so a single released non-conforming batch or a missed expedited safety report could produce losses well above that.
- **The § 8.1 indemnity is narrow.** It does cover breach of Section 5, but ordinary negligent performance of other Services (e.g., distribution under A-5, data migration under A-7) is only indemnified if it rises to gross negligence.

**Recommended fix:**
- Carve breaches of § 5 (Regulatory and Quality Matters) and violations of Applicable Law out of the § 8.3 cap.
- Alternatively, raise the cap to the greater of total Service Fees and a fixed amount, e.g., $[10] million.
- Confirm in TSA § 8.3 that the cap does not limit any claim under the APA, including where the same facts give rise to both.

Proposed addition to TSA § 8.3:

> "Nothing in this Section 8.3 limits any right or remedy of Buyer under the Purchase Agreement."

---

## Issue 4: Knowledge qualifiers on CMO-related regulatory and recall representations

**Where:** APA § 4.5(c) (CMO notices "to Seller's knowledge"); APA § 4.7 ("to Seller's knowledge no facts exist").

**Why it matters to Vaikiv:**
- The CMO (Brennholt) is the source of the known compliance history, including the June 2025 Form 483 and the moisture deviation.
- Knowledge-qualifying CMO notices lets Seller avoid liability for FDA correspondence the CMO received but did not pass on.
- "Knowledge" is not defined in § 1.1. That leaves it open whether knowledge means actual knowledge of named individuals or includes constructive knowledge.

**Recommended fix:**
- Add a defined "Seller's Knowledge": the actual knowledge of [named heads of quality, regulatory and supply chain] after reasonable inquiry, including of the CMO under the Quality Agreement.
- Remove the knowledge qualifier from § 4.5(c) for communications that the CMO was obliged to forward to Seller under the Quality Agreement.

---

## Issue 5: Escrow sizing and release mechanics

**Where:** APA §§ 2.6, 2.7, 9.6; Escrow §§ 2.1, 4.1, 4.2.

**Points:**
- **Size.** The escrow is $18.6 million, equal to the 10% Cap. That is market-standard for a capped-rep escrow, but its value depends entirely on the release date fixed under Issue 1.
- **Order of recovery.** APA § 9.6 requires recovery from escrow first, then from Seller directly. That is acceptable, provided the § 2.7 "not the exclusive source" language stays.
- **Objection mechanics.** The 20-Business-Day deemed-acceptance mechanic in Escrow § 4.2(c) is buyer-favourable. Keep it.

**Recommended fix:**
- Conform the Release Date to the new survival period (see Issue 1).
- Confirm that Pending Claim Amounts are retained on release (this is already in § 4.1).

---

## Issue 6: Closing press release

**Where:** Joint Press Release.

**Points:**
- **Consistency.** The release is consistent with the deal documents: $186,000,000 purchase price, March 2, 2026 Closing, NDA 214-883, and a nine-month TSA. Consistent with APA § 10.2 and TSA § 7.1, I see no substantive legal issue.
- **Patent statement.** The statement that Oravexin has a "durable patent position" should be confirmed by Vaikiv's IP and IR teams. The listed patents expire in 2036 and 2037 and one application is pending. The statement should be defensible against any Paragraph IV challenge risk.
